title: Ezra 7:11–28
context: This unit gives the copy of the letter King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra (7:11–26), followed by Ezra’s own words of praise (7:27–28). The letter, generally recognized as written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, authorizes any willing Israelites, priests, and Levites to go with Ezra, commissions him to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of his God, provides silver, gold, and supplies for the temple’s sacrifices and needs, exempts temple personnel from taxes, and authorizes Ezra to appoint judges and teach the law beyond the River. With 7:27 the narrative shifts into Ezra’s first-person voice, which continues through chapter 8. Ezra blesses the LORD “who has put such a thing as this in the king’s heart” and credits his strength to “the LORD my God’s hand on me” (7:27–28). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God governs the hearts of kings for the good of his people, and Ezra responds with praise rather than self-congratulation.

verses.text: Now this is the copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, even the scribe of the words of the LORD’s commandments, and of his statutes to Israel:
verses.arminianNotes: This is the copy of the letter Artaxerxes gave to Ezra, priest and scribe of the LORD’s commandments. Arminian readers note that the narrator presents the letter as an official document, emphasizing Ezra’s role as an expert in God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the honor given to Ezra’s office and see God using the Persian court to equip his servant. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the king’s authorization and as highlighting Ezra’s calling to the law of God.

verses.text: Artaxerxes, king of kings, To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the perfect God of heaven. Now
verses.arminianNotes: Artaxerxes, “king of kings,” addresses Ezra as scribe of the law of “the perfect God of heaven.” Arminian readers note that a pagan king speaks respectfully of Israel’s God. Whatever the king’s motives, his letter opens the way for Ezra’s mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony of a self-styled king of kings writing to support the worship of the true God, who rules over all kings. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an official greeting and decline to speculate about the king’s personal faith beyond what the text states.

verses.text: I make a decree that all those of the people of Israel and their priests and the Levites in my realm, who intend of their own free will to go to Jerusalem, go with you.
verses.arminianNotes: The king decrees that any Israelites, priests, or Levites in his realm who wish to go to Jerusalem may go with Ezra. Arminian readers note the emphasis on free will: no one is forced to go. The return is an invitation to be accepted or declined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the voluntary character of the return and see God moving willing hearts to respond. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an open invitation, and neither turns the king’s phrase “of their own free will” into a doctrinal argument about the will.

verses.text: Because you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to inquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem, according to the law of your God which is in your hand,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra is sent by the king and his seven counselors to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of his God, “which is in your hand.” Arminian readers note that Ezra carries God’s law as the standard for his mission, and that the king recognizes it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the law as the measure of Ezra’s work and note the king’s official sanction. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing God’s law at the center of the restored community, and both see the king’s authority serving that purpose.

verses.text: and to carry the silver and gold, which the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra is to carry silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, “whose habitation is in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note the generosity of the gift and the recognition of Jerusalem as the place of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing for his house through the treasury of a foreign king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of God supplying the needs of his people’s worship through unexpected means, without speculating about the king’s inner motives.

verses.text: and all the silver and gold that you will find in all the province of Babylon, with the free will offering of the people and of the priests, offering willingly for the house of their God which is in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra may also collect silver and gold from the province of Babylon, along with freewill offerings from the people and priests. Arminian readers note the willing generosity of those who stay behind. Giving is a way to share in the work even for those who do not go.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the combination of royal provision and freewill offerings. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring willing giving for God’s house and see in it a community supporting the restoration together, whether they travel or remain.

verses.text: Therefore you shall with all diligence buy with this money bulls, rams, and lambs with their meal offerings and their drink offerings, and shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God which is in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra is to buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their meal and drink offerings, for the altar in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the king’s gifts are directed to worship, not to Ezra’s personal use. The resources serve the sacrifices God commanded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the provision directed to the ordered worship God gave Israel. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as ensuring that the gifts serve God’s house, and neither builds a further argument on the specific offerings named.

verses.text: Whatever seems good to you and to your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and the gold, do that according to the will of your God.
verses.arminianNotes: Whatever seems good to Ezra and his brothers to do with the rest, they may do “according to the will of your God.” Arminian readers note the trust placed in Ezra’s judgment, exercised within God’s will. Responsibility is given, along with freedom to use it well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the king places Ezra’s discretion under the will of God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of stewardship guided by God’s will, and both see in it the king’s respect for the God of Israel.

verses.text: The vessels that are given to you for the service of the house of your God, deliver before the God of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The vessels given for the service of God’s house are to be delivered before the God of Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the care for sacred objects entrusted to Ezra. Faithful delivery of these vessels will be part of Ezra’s responsibility on the journey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vessels as consecrated to God’s service and note how carefully they will be handled in chapter 8. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the provision for worship and as preparing for the account of their safe delivery.

verses.text: Whatever more will be needed for the house of your God, which you may have occasion to give, give it out of the king’s treasure house.
verses.arminianNotes: Anything else needed for God’s house may be given from the king’s treasury. Arminian readers note the generosity of the provision, which removes obstacles to the work. God’s people receive what they need to complete their task.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s abundant provision through the king’s resources. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the remarkable support given to Ezra and see in it God’s care for his house, without making the king a model of faith.

verses.text: I, even I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers who are beyond the River, that whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, requires of you, it shall be done with all diligence,
verses.arminianNotes: Artaxerxes decrees to the treasurers beyond the River that whatever Ezra requires is to be done diligently. Arminian readers note that the king’s authority now works on Ezra’s behalf. Officials who might have hindered the work are instructed to support it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God turning the machinery of empire to serve his purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence of God’s gracious provision through earthly authorities, and both see in it the fulfillment of God’s care for the restored community.

verses.text: up to one hundred talents of silver, and to one hundred cors of wheat, and to one hundred baths of wine, and to one hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.
verses.arminianNotes: The king sets limits: up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, one hundred baths of wine and oil, and salt without limit. Arminian readers note the generous yet defined provision, which shows careful administration alongside generosity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a lavish provision for God’s house within the structures of royal government. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail of the king’s support and decline to build doctrine on the quantities.

verses.text: Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven, let it be done exactly for the house of the God of heaven; for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons?
verses.arminianNotes: Whatever the God of heaven commands is to be done exactly, “for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons?” Arminian readers note that the king acts partly from concern to avoid divine wrath. His motive is recorded honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the king’s fear of wrath and see God working through even mixed motives to accomplish his purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing the king’s reasoning without endorsing it as true faith, and both see God’s purpose served through it.

verses.text: Also we inform you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, or laborers of this house of God.
verses.arminianNotes: No tribute, custom, or toll is to be imposed on priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, or other workers of God’s house. Arminian readers note the practical relief this provides, freeing temple personnel to serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the exemption as God’s provision for the ministry of his house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a practical arrangement that supported worship, and neither finds a doctrinal dispute in the tax exemption.

verses.text: You, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people who are beyond the River, who all know the laws of your God; and teach him who doesn’t know them.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra is to appoint magistrates and judges who know the laws of his God, and to teach those who do not know them. Arminian readers note the importance of teaching. Knowledge of God’s law must be passed on, so that people can understand and obey it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priority of teaching and note that the king refers to “the wisdom of your God that is in your hand.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing instruction in God’s law at the heart of the community’s life, a theme that matches Ezra’s own resolve in 7:10.

verses.text: Whoever will not do the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be executed on him with all diligence, whether it is to death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever will not obey the law of God and the law of the king is to be punished, by death, banishment, confiscation, or imprisonment. Arminian readers note that the king’s decree joins civil penalties to the law. The verse records Persian policy without commending it as a model.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing the king’s legal framework, not as a pattern for the church today. Shared ground: both traditions read it as historical description of the authority granted to Ezra, and both handle the penalties soberly without expanding them.

verses.text: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put such a thing as this in the king’s heart, to beautify the LORD’s house which is in Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra blesses the LORD, the God of the fathers, “who has put such a thing as this in the king’s heart.” Arminian readers see God influencing the king’s heart while the king freely issues his decree. Ezra’s praise rightly credits God for the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God directing the king’s heart effectively to accomplish his purpose for his house. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God moved the king and that praise belongs to him; how God governs human hearts is treated in existing providence discussions, and no new contrast is added here.

verses.text: and has extended loving kindness to me before the king and his counselors, and before all the king’s mighty princes. I was strengthened according to the LORD my God’s hand on me, and I gathered together chief men out of Israel to go up with me.
verses.arminianNotes: God has extended loving kindness to Ezra before the king and his officials, and Ezra, strengthened by the LORD’s hand, gathers leaders to go with him. Arminian readers note that God’s favor gives Ezra courage to act. He responds by taking initiative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s kindness and strength as the source of Ezra’s action. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Ezra’s humble confession that his success came from God, and both see in it a pattern of grace received and then put to work in faithful service.
